signs.text: Your boss uses your first name when you come in, and it is the right one.
Your boss turns to you in front of everyone and asks what you think. Your boss listens to all of it.
Your boss moves a folder off the chair next to the one at the head of the table. It might be for you. It might be that the folder was finished.
Your boss nods in your direction when you sit down. It could be a greeting. It could be the slide.
Your boss says that you will be copied in. Nobody says on what.
Your boss is cheerful with the whole room. You are in the room.
Your boss refers to you as "our colleague here". It may be that the name has slipped your boss's mind.
You begin a sentence. Your boss finishes it, differently, and moves to the next slide.
Your boss asks you a question, then checks the answer with someone else while you are still giving it.

believer: Your boss looks faintly embarrassed, and asks whether you had a view of your own.
Your boss thanks you, and asks what you actually think. There is a pause in which you could have said.
incompetent: Your boss glows, and tells the room that this is exactly the sort of thing your boss has been saying.
Your boss repeats what you said about your boss, to someone who was standing next to you when you said it.
practitioner: Your boss gives you a small nod, as one gives a tip, and remembers it.
Your boss says nothing, and a week later your name is on a list you wanted to be on.

believer: Your boss waits until it is over, then asks what it means in practice. You can see that a real answer was hoped for.
Your boss writes something down, then crosses it out, and looks a little tired.
incompetent: Your boss is visibly thrilled, and asks you to send it over, and to say it again more slowly.
Your boss says that this is the kind of confidence the floor needs. Your boss has not understood it, and likes it better for that.
practitioner: Your boss recognises the workmanship, and asks whether it could be made to say that it was your boss's idea.
Your boss smiles at the right moment, for the room, and makes a note of what you are capable of.

believer: Your boss reads it properly, and stops at your desk to say that it was good work. It takes you a moment to work out what is happening.
Your boss asks you how you did it, and listens to the answer.
incompetent: Your boss asks whether there is a version with fewer words in it, and more of a story.
Your boss says thanks, and asks when you will be doing something with more visibility.
practitioner: Your boss takes it upstairs that afternoon. Your name has come off it on the way.
Your boss thanks you, and shows it to the floor above as a thing that your boss's team has done.

believer: Your boss looks at the chart for some time, then says thank you, and means it. Your boss asks what you would need to fix it.
Your boss closes the door and asks you to go through it again. Nobody has closed that door to listen before.
incompetent: Your boss looks at the chart as one looks at a wasp, and asks whether it could be presented in a more positive colour.
Your boss asks who else has seen this, then says that it has come as a complete surprise, to the room.
practitioner: Your boss looks at you, not the chart, and thanks you for your candour. You have never been thanked so quietly.
Your boss asks who else has seen this, and writes the answer down, with your name above it.

believer: Your boss seems pleased to see you, and asks when you will be getting back to your project.
Your boss thanks you, and insists on paying separately.
incompetent: Your boss is delighted to have you there, and tells you the one about the fax machine again.
Your boss says that you are good value, and asks what it is that you do.
practitioner: Your boss looks at you for slightly longer than usual, and buys you the next one. Something has been entered in a ledger.
Your boss says that this will not be forgotten, in the tone of someone who forgets nothing.

believer: Your boss asks, mildly, whether there was a reason you did not come to your boss first. It is a real question, and you have no answer.
Your boss looks hurt, and tries not to, and is not good at it.
incompetent: Your boss is flustered, and asks several people what you said, and whether it was about your boss.
Your boss starts copying you in on everything, in case that was the problem.
practitioner: Your boss says nothing at all, and smiles when you next meet. You would rather have been shouted at.
Your boss congratulates you on your initiative, in writing, and keeps a copy.

believer: Your boss asks whether anyone has checked that, and looks at you while asking.
Your boss frowns, and says that this is not what the session is for. Your boss seems to believe that.
incompetent: Your boss writes it down with visible relief. It was not your boss's fault, then.
Your boss nods along and says that this is what your boss had suspected all along.
practitioner: Your boss gives you a look of mild professional recognition, and moves on.
Your boss notes how quickly you found someone, and how cleanly.

believer: Your boss stops you afterwards to say that it was decent of you, and asks what really happened.
Your boss seems troubled by it, and asks if you are all right.
incompetent: Your boss looks relieved, without being sure why, and moves to the next slide.
Your boss thanks you for your ownership, a word your boss heard on Tuesday.
practitioner: Your boss thanks you warmly for your ownership, in front of everyone, and makes sure that it is minuted.
Your boss looks at you with new interest, as one looks at somewhere to put things.
